questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes IPsec tunnel mode from transport mode?

options.text: Tunnel wraps the whole original packet
options.rationale: Correct: a new outer header is added; transport mode protects the payload only.

options.text: Tunnel mode is used between sites
options.rationale: Its typical use, but not what makes it different.

options.text: Transport mode encrypts more of the packet
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: Tunnel mode uses AH; transport uses ESP
options.rationale: Either protocol can run in either mode.

questions.explanation: ESP uses symmetric ciphers, with keys negotiated via IKE using Diffie-Hellman. Tunnel mode encapsulates the whole original packet (site-to-site); transport mode protects the payload only.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tunnel = whole packet; transport = payload only.

questions.stem: Two labs must exchange multicast routing updates across a router path that forwards unicast traffic alone, and encryption isn't required. Which tunnel BEST fits?

options.text: A plain GRE tunnel
options.rationale: Correct: GRE carries multicast inside unicast; nothing more is needed.

options.text: GRE over IPsec
options.rationale: Would work, but adds encryption overhead nobody asked for.

options.text: An IPsec crypto map
options.rationale: A policy-based crypto map doesn't carry multicast.

options.text: A remote-access SSL VPN
options.rationale: User VPNs don't connect lab routers.

questions.explanation: GRE (IP protocol 47) is encapsulation that can carry many protocols, including multicast and routing protocols. It is flexible but provides no encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: GRE carries multicast and routing protocols; no encryption.

questions.stem: In a GRE over IPsec design, which part provides which function?

options.text: GRE carries multicast; IPsec encrypts
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: IPsec carries multicast; GRE encrypts
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: Both encrypt, for double protection
options.rationale: GRE doesn't encrypt.

options.text: GRE authenticates; IPsec routes
options.rationale: Neither describes what each part actually does.

questions.explanation: GRE over IPsec protects a GRE tunnel with IPsec: GRE adds multiprotocol and multicast support, and IPsec adds encryption.
questions.discriminator_tested: GRE adds multicast; IPsec adds encryption.

questions.stem: Cisco DMVPN is built from several technologies. Which two of these does it use? (Choose two.)

options.text: mGRE
options.rationale: Correct: multipoint GRE lets one interface reach many spokes.

options.text: NHRP
options.rationale: Correct: spokes use it to find each other's addresses.

options.text: TACACS+
options.rationale: An AAA protocol, not part of DMVPN.

options.text: Static NAT
options.rationale: Not a DMVPN component.
Port access control, unrelated to DMVPN.

questions.explanation: Cisco DMVPN is a hub-and-spoke VPN with dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels, built from mGRE, NHRP, and IPsec. It scales without configuring a full mesh.

questions.stem: What BEST describes what the configuration below creates?
questions.exhibit:
interface Tunnel10
 ip address 172.31.0.1 255.255.255.252
 tunnel source g0/0
 tunnel destination 203.0.113.2
 tunnel mode ipsec ipv4
 tunnel protection ipsec profile SITE-B

options.text: A route-based IPsec VTI, with no GRE header
options.rationale: Correct: 'tunnel mode ipsec ipv4' makes a VTI.

options.text: An encrypted tunnel to 203.0.113.2
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say what kind of tunnel.

options.text: A GRE tunnel protected by IPsec
options.rationale: GRE over IPsec would use 'tunnel mode gre'.

options.text: A DMVPN spoke with dynamic tunnels
options.rationale: DMVPN uses mGRE and NHRP.

questions.explanation: A Cisco IPsec VTI is an IPsec tunnel presented as a routable virtual interface: route-based, with no GRE header. Crypto maps are policy-based.

options.text: The whole key trust system
options.rationale: Correct: CAs, certificates, policies, and processes together.

options.text: A server that issues certificates
options.rationale: That is a CA, one component.

options.text: A single certificate used for a website
options.rationale: A certificate is one product of PKI.

options.text: A symmetric key shared among users
options.rationale: PKI is built on public/private key pairs.

questions.explanation: Public key infrastructure (PKI) is the framework of CAs, certificates, policies, and processes that bind public keys to identities. It is the whole trust system, not one component.
questions.discriminator_tested: PKI is the whole trust system.

questions.stem: A browser shows the certificate path below. What BEST explains why it trusts portal.example.com's certificate?
questions.exhibit:
Certificate path
  Example Root CA          (in the trusted root store)
    Example Issuing CA
      portal.example.com

options.text: It chains to a root CA the browser already trusts
options.rationale: Correct: each certificate is signed by the one above it, up to a trusted root.

options.text: It was issued by Example Issuing CA
options.rationale: True, but that CA is trusted only because the root signed it.

options.text: The website sent its private key for checking
options.rationale: Private keys are never sent.

options.text: Certificates on HTTPS sites are trusted automatically
options.rationale: Untrusted chains trigger warnings.

questions.explanation: Certificate authorities are trusted entities that issue, sign, and revoke certificates. The root CA is the trust anchor, signing with its own private key.
questions.discriminator_tested: The CA is the trust anchor.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a certificate template from a certificate?

options.text: It's the blueprint; certificates are issued from it
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Templates are stored on the CA
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't explain the difference.

options.text: A template holds a private key; a certificate doesn't
options.rationale: Templates hold settings, not keys.

options.text: They are the same document in different formats
options.rationale: A template is settings; a certificate is a signed document.

questions.explanation: A certificate template holds the predefined settings (key usage, validity, key size, subject fields) a CA applies when issuing certificates. It is the blueprint for issuance, not a certificate itself.

questions.stem: Which two checks does a client make when validating a server's certificate? (Choose two.)

options.text: That a trusted CA's signature is valid
options.rationale: Correct: the signature proves who issued it.

options.text: That the current date is within its validity
options.rationale: Correct: expired or not-yet-valid certificates fail.

options.text: That the certificate includes the private key
options.rationale: Certificates never contain the private key.

options.text: That the server's password is correct
options.rationale: Certificates don't involve passwords.

options.text: That the certificate is under 1 KB
options.rationale: Size isn't a validation check.

questions.explanation: Certificates are signed X.509 documents binding a public key to an identity. They are validated by the CA's signature, the validity dates, and revocation status, and they never hold the private key.
questions.discriminator_tested: Validated by CA signature, dates, and revocation status.

questions.stem: The entry 'access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0' was meant to permit the 192.168.1.0/24 network. What BEST describes the problem?

options.text: Subnet mask used, not wildcard
options.rationale: Correct: the wildcard should be 0.0.0.255.

options.text: It won't match the intended hosts
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

options.text: A standard ACL needs the 'tcp' keyword
options.rationale: Standard ACLs take no protocol.

options.text: ACL 10 is reserved for extended ACLs
options.rationale: 1-99 are standard numbers.

questions.explanation: Standard ACL commands take a number, an action, and a source plus wildcard. A subnet mask used in place of a wildcard matches the wrong bits.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standard ACL: number, action, source plus wildcard.

questions.stem: Which traffic does the entry 'access-list 110 permit tcp host 10.1.4.20 10.1.9.0 0.0.0.255 eq 22' permit?

options.rationale: Correct: source host, destination subnet, TCP 22.
Source comes before destination; this is reversed.

options.text: Any traffic from 10.1.4.20 to 10.1.9.0/24
options.rationale: The port limits it to TCP 22.
Telnet is TCP 23.

questions.explanation: Extended ACL commands follow the order action, protocol, source, destination, then port.
questions.discriminator_tested: Order: action, protocol, source, destination, port.

questions.stem: Which command sequence creates a named extended ACL that permits HTTPS from anywhere?

options.text: ip access-list extended WEB-IN, then permit tcp any any eq 443
options.rationale: Correct: the type keyword, then entries without 'access-list'.

options.text: ip access-list WEB-IN, then permit tcp any any eq 443
options.rationale: The 'extended' keyword is required.

options.text: ip access-list extended WEB-IN, then access-list permit tcp any any eq 443
options.rationale: Named ACL entries omit 'access-list'.

options.text: access-list WEB-IN permit tcp any any eq 443
options.rationale: Names are used with 'ip access-list', not this syntax.

questions.explanation: Named ACLs start with 'ip access-list extended NAME' (or 'standard'), then take entries such as 'permit tcp any any eq 443' in ACL config mode. Entries omit the 'access-list' keyword.
questions.discriminator_tested: Named ACLs need the type keyword; entries omit 'access-list'.

questions.stem: ACL 110 must filter traffic arriving at the router from the user LAN on interface g0/1. Which command applies it correctly?

options.text: ip access-group 110 in, under interface g0/1
options.rationale: Correct: 'in' is traffic entering the router on g0/1.

options.text: ip access-group 110 out, under interface g0/1
options.rationale: 'out' filters traffic leaving toward the users.

options.text: access-class 110 in, under line vty 0 4
options.rationale: That limits management sessions, not traffic.

options.text: ip access-group 110 in, in global config
options.rationale: access-group is an interface command.

questions.explanation: An ACL is applied with 'interface g0/1' then 'ip access-group 110 in' (or out). Direction is relative to the router, there is one ACL per protocol, interface, and direction, and an unapplied ACL filters nothing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Direction is relative to the router.

options.text: It limits sessions to the device
options.rationale: Correct: it controls who can log in to the router itself.

options.text: access-class is applied under line configuration
options.rationale: True, but where it is typed isn't what it does.

options.text: access-class filters traffic passing through
options.rationale: That is ip access-group.

options.text: access-class requires a named ACL
options.rationale: Numbered ACLs work too.

questions.explanation: Applying an ACL to VTY lines uses 'access-class 10 in'. access-class limits management sessions to the device; ip access-group filters traffic through an interface.
questions.discriminator_tested: access-class = sessions to the device; access-group = traffic through.

questions.stem: An engineer adds 'access-list 110 deny tcp any any eq 23' to numbered ACL 110, which ends with 'permit ip any any'. Telnet still works. What BEST explains why?

options.text: The new entry was appended after the permit-all
options.rationale: Correct: new numbered entries go to the end, below the broad permit.

options.text: The permit matches Telnet first
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why the deny sits below it.

options.text: Numbered ACLs ignore entries added later
options.rationale: They accept them, at the end.

options.text: Telnet uses UDP 23, so it doesn't match
options.rationale: Telnet is TCP 23.

questions.explanation: New numbered entries append to the end; sequence numbers allow inserting entries. A broad entry above a specific one shadows it.
questions.discriminator_tested: New entries append to the end; a broad entry shadows a later specific one.

questions.stem: Which entry body matches both SSH and Telnet in one line?

options.text: tcp any any range 22 23
options.rationale: Correct: 'range' with tcp covers both ports.

options.text: ip any any range 22 23
options.rationale: 'ip' can't take ports.

options.text: udp any any range 22 23
options.rationale: SSH and Telnet use TCP.

options.text: tcp any any gt 23
options.rationale: Matches ports above 23, missing both.

questions.explanation: Port and protocol keywords: protocols tcp, udp, icmp, ip; operators eq, neq, gt, lt, range. Ports require tcp or udp; 'ip' can't take ports.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ports require tcp or udp; range for spans.

questions.stem: Interface g0/1 connects to the server LAN where 10.1.9.10 lives. Users' Telnet sessions to 10.1.9.10 still succeed, and the output below shows entry 10 with 0 matches. What is the MOST likely explanation?
questions.exhibit:
R1# show access-lists 110
Extended IP access list 110
    10 deny tcp any host 10.1.9.10 eq 23 (0 matches)
    20 permit ip any any (15233 matches)
R1# show ip interface g0/1 | include access list
  Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is 110

options.text: It's applied in the wrong direction
options.rationale: Correct: requests to the server leave g0/1 outbound; inbound sees only replies.

options.text: Entry 10 isn't matching any packets
options.rationale: True, but that's the symptom, not the cause.

options.text: The permit entry overrides the deny
options.rationale: The deny is first; order isn't the problem.

options.text: The ACL isn't applied to any interface
options.rationale: The output shows it applied inbound on g0/1.

questions.explanation: When verifying ACLs, 'show access-lists' shows what the ACL says and its hits, and 'show ip interface' shows where it is applied. Zero hits on a deny that should match points to placement or direction.
questions.discriminator_tested: show access-lists = contents and hits; show ip interface = where applied.

questions.stem: Which command adds a note to ACL 110 explaining why an entry exists?

options.text: access-list 110 remark Block Telnet
options.rationale: Correct: 'remark' documents the ACL in the configuration.

options.text: access-list 110 description Block Telnet
options.rationale: 'description' is an interface command.

options.text: ! Block Telnet
options.rationale: A '!' comment isn't saved in the configuration.

options.text: no access-list 110
options.rationale: That deletes the whole ACL.

questions.explanation: 'remark' documents an entry. 'no ip access-group 110 in' removes only the application, while 'no access-list 110' deletes the whole ACL.
questions.discriminator_tested: remark documents; removing the application vs deleting the ACL.
